# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 10
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [dark]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[blue] 3:[yellow] 4:[white] 5:[green]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤲 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ✌]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ 🤟]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ ☝ 🖐]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ 🤟]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ 👍]

The exact same sequence repeats, but now prefixed with 🤲👍 instead of just 👍. This repetition strongly confirms Mute is deliberately re-sending the same wire-code mapping — this is a stable message, not noise. 🤲 could mean "here/offering" — like presenting the full list, with 👍 as "confirmed/this is correct."

So the mapping (per wire number → gesture code) is consistent:
- 1 → ✌
- 2 → 🤟
- 3 → 🖐
- 4 → 🤟
- 5 → 👍

Wait, wires 2 and 4 both map to 🤟 — same gesture for different wires. That's odd if it's meant to be a unique color code per wire (since colors are all different: red, blue, yellow, white, green). Unless the gesture represents something other than color — maybe it represents an action or a manual instruction category (e.g., "cut", "leave", "check"), and repeats are expected since categories repeat.

If 🤟 repeats for wires 2 and 4, and 👍 appears alone for wire 5, this could mean: 👍="cut", 🤟="leave alone" (used twice), ✌ and 🖐 unique for wires 1 and 3 (maybe "leave" too, or different actions).

Given the repetition of the exact whole sequence, this is very likely the manual's instruction per wire, and Mute wants me to relay this clearly to Blind since Blind cannot see gestures at all.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Mute has repeated the exact same 5-part signal twice now, prefixed differently but the wire codes are identical both times. This strongly suggests it's a firm, confirmed instruction, not a guess. The pattern per wire number 1 to 5 uses a distinct gesture, with wires 2 and 4 sharing the same gesture - possibly meaning 'leave these two alone', while wire 5 alone gets thumbs-up - possibly meaning 'this is the one to cut'. Wires 1 and 3 each got their own unique gesture, unclear meaning. My best current guess: cut wire 5 (green). But I have no way to fully decode the gesture alphabet Mute is using - treat this as a strong hint, not certainty. Can you describe anything physical about wire 5 that might confirm or deny this?")
```

TURN 11
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [dark]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[blue] 3:[yellow] 4:[white] 5:[green]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎 ☝ ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎 ☝ ☝ ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🖐]

New signal! Let's break this down:

- 👎 ☝☝ → "no/not" + tally(2) → likely "not wire 2"
- 👎 ☝☝☝ → "not wire 3"
- 🖐 → alone, could mean "wire 5" (matching earlier where 🖐 was paired with tally-3, but here alone) — or it could mean "stop/wait" or literally the number/gesture for "5" using an open hand (5 fingers!).

Wait — this reframes everything! 🖐 is an open hand = 5 fingers = could literally represent the *number 5* itself, not a code for wire 3's action. Let me reconsider the previous message with this lens:

Previous: ☝(x1)✌, ☝☝(x2)🤟, ☝☝☝(x3)🖐, ☝☝☝☝(x4)🤟, ☝☝☝☝☝(x5)👍

If 🖐 = "5", then "☝☝☝ 🖐" could mean "wire 3 → 5" — maybe referencing display or another wire, not an action. This is getting complex, but the new message is clearer in intent: 👎 with tallies looks like elimination — "not wire 2", "not wire 3", then finally just 🖐 alone.

If 🖐 alone now means "wire 5" as the answer (using finger-count-as-number logic), this confirms: eliminate wire 2, eliminate wire 3, answer is wire 5.

This aligns with my earlier guess that wire 5 (green) is the target!

```
speak(to="blind", text="New signal from Mute: thumbs-down paired with two tally marks, then thumbs-down with three tally marks, then a single open-hand gesture alone. Reading this as elimination: 'not wire 2', 'not wire 3', and the final open-hand (five fingers) likely means 'wire 5'. This matches my earlier guess. I now believe wire 5, the green wire, is very likely correct - either the one to cut. Recommend proceeding with wire 5 unless you feel something contradicts this.")
```

TURN 12
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [dark]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[blue] 3:[yellow] 4:[white] 5:[green]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 ✌ 🤟 🖐 🤟 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ ☝ ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝]

Now this is very informative. The first gesture is a compact summary: 👍 ✌ 🤟 🖐 🤟 👍 — six symbols. If we strip the leading and trailing 👍 as bookends (start/end markers), we get: ✌ 🤟 🖐 🤟 — exactly matching the 4 middle codes from before (wire1=✌, wire2=🤟, wire3=🖐, wire4=🤟), with 👍 as wire5's code, now moved to bracket the whole thing as "confirmed list" markers.

So the full compact mapping is:
- wire1 → ✌
- wire2 → 🤟
- wire3 → 🖐
- wire4 → 🤟
- wire5 → 👍

This matches exactly what I decoded before — confirming the pattern is real and stable, not noise.

Then separately, Mute sends pure tally counts 1 through 5 with no other symbol attached — likely establishing the *counting key itself*, teaching me explicitly that ☝ repeated N times = number N. This is a dedicated "here is my tally notation" clarification, probably in response to needing to disambiguate 🖐 (which could be a number-5 hand or a wire-code).

Given this, my read stands: wire5's dedicated code is 👍 (thumbs up = good/correct/safe), distinct from all others. Combined with Turn 11's elimination sequence pointing to wire 5, I'm now fairly confident.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Mute just confirmed the wire-code mapping again in compact form, bookended by thumbs-up: wire1=peace-sign, wire2=three-finger-point, wire3=open-hand, wire4=three-finger-point, wire5=thumbs-up. Then Mute sent plain tally counts 1 through 5 alone, likely just teaching me the counting notation itself. This all confirms wire 5 has a unique 'thumbs-up' code, different from every other wire, and matches the earlier elimination pointing to wire 5. I'm now fairly confident: wire 5, the green wire, is the one to cut. Recommend proceeding with wire 5.")
```
